opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, the lottery ticket hypothesis came out of a fairly simple habit: when someone makes a claim in deep learning, try the most direct experiment you can think of that would prove it wrong.

At the time, the conventional wisdom about pruning was that you could train a big network, remove most of its weights, and keep the accuracy. But if you took that smaller, sparse architecture and trained it from scratch, it didn't work as well. The usual explanation was that you needed the overparameterization to train successfully, and that small networks were just hard to optimize.

I'm a bit stubborn about these things, and I wanted to know *why*. So instead of just accepting it, I asked a very literal question: what if, when you retrain the pruned network, you don't use a fresh random initialization? What if you reset the surviving weights back to the exact values they had at the start of training? That was a cheap experiment, and it was the kind of thing you can just try in an afternoon. And it worked. Those sparse subnetworks trained to the same accuracy as the full network, sometimes faster. If you reinitialized them randomly, they fell apart. That contrast was the whole finding: the initialization mattered, not just the structure.

A lot of my approach is about that kind of control. You need to know what happens when you change exactly one thing. Re-randomizing was the control that made the result meaningful. Without it, you'd just have another pruning paper.

The other thing that shaped it was being willing to follow the result when it broke. On small networks like LeNet and small convnets on CIFAR, rewinding to initialization worked beautifully. On bigger networks like ResNets on ImageNet, it didn't. It would have been tempting to tuck that away. Instead, that failure led to the work on rewinding to an early point in training rather than iteration zero, and to the stability analysis around linear mode connectivity. It turned out that after a small amount of training, the network becomes stable to the noise of SGD, and that's roughly when lottery tickets start to show up. So the failure case actually taught us more about the training dynamics than the success did.

I also try to be honest about what the hypothesis is and isn't. It was never a practical recipe for faster training. Finding these tickets with iterative magnitude pruning is incredibly expensive, because you train the network over and over. It was a scientific observation about how neural networks learn, and I think the value came from treating it that way: careful experiments, lots of baselines, and a willingness to say "here's where this stops working."

If there's a general lesson, it's that deep learning rewards empirical science. We don't have the theory to tell us what's true in advance, so the best thing you can do is design clean experiments, run the boring controls, and take the surprises seriously instead of explaining them away.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts pruning a trained network with training the resulting sparse architecture from scratch, then asks why and tests whether restoring the original surviving weights explains the difference.

r002.rationale: It describes directly testing a claim in deep learning, challenging the received explanation about overparameterization with a controlled experiment, and following up on unexpected results.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the lottery ticket hypothesis came out of a very empirical, almost stubborn way of working, rather than out of a grand theory.

When I started my PhD at MIT, I came from a systems and security background, and I didn't have a lot of the deep learning intuition that people who'd been in the field for years had. What I did have was a habit of asking really simple questions and then just running the experiment instead of reasoning about it from the armchair. The question that started all of this was embarrassingly basic: we know you can prune a trained network down to a tiny fraction of its weights and it still works. So why can't we just train that small network from the start? Everyone I asked had an answer, and the answers were all slightly different, and none of them came with evidence. That was the signal to me that nobody actually knew.

So the approach was: pick the smallest setting where the question is meaningful, which for us was a little fully connected network on MNIST, and try the obvious things one at a time. Train, prune, reset the remaining weights to random, retrain. That fails. Then the thing that felt almost silly: reset the remaining weights to the exact values they had at initialization, and retrain. And that worked. Michael Carbin, my advisor, and I spent a long time trying to break it before we believed it, because the result was so clean that my first instinct was that we had a bug.

That skepticism was really important to how the work developed. A lot of what came after, the stuff about rewinding to an early iteration rather than iteration zero, and the trouble getting the original version to work on larger networks like ResNets on ImageNet, came from us pushing on our own result until it cracked and then trying to understand why. I think if I'd been more invested in the hypothesis as a theory, I would have been tempted to defend it instead of stress-testing it. Treating it as a set of empirical claims that had to survive every experiment we could throw at them is what made it hold up, and also what made the limitations clear.

The other piece is scale of experimentation. I was running enormous numbers of trials, with multiple seeds, varying one thing at a time, and being pretty religious about reporting error bars. That sounds mundane, but a lot of the confusion in the pruning literature at the time came from people comparing single runs. Having that discipline meant that when something surprising showed up, we could trust it, and when something didn't replicate, we could say so.

So I'd summarize it as: ask a question simple enough that you're embarrassed to ask it, run the experiment rather than argue about it, and then try as hard as you can to prove yourself wrong before you tell anyone else.

r001.rationale: The candidate asks why a network that works after pruning cannot simply be trained in its smaller form from the start, capturing the question of why pruning seemed to work only after training.

r002.rationale: The candidate says prevailing explanations lacked evidence, then describes testing the question experimentally and stress-testing the result rather than relying on received wisdom.

astra-6.text:
My approach was pretty empirical: take an idea, turn it into an experiment, and see where it breaks. With the lottery ticket hypothesis, the starting point was this puzzling observation that you could train a neural network and then remove a huge fraction of its weights without losing much accuracy. That raises a natural question: if such a small network can do the job, why couldn’t we have trained that small network in the first place?

So the experiment was to train a network, prune it, and then try training the remaining network again. The crucial distinction was whether we gave that smaller network a fresh random initialization or reset its surviving weights to the values they had at the beginning of the original training run. Resetting them to their original values made a surprising difference. That suggested we weren’t just finding a good network structure; we were finding a structure together with an initialization that made it train well.

That’s where the lottery ticket idea came from: perhaps a large randomly initialized network contains smaller subnetworks that are already well positioned to learn. The hypothesis grew out of that experimental distinction. And then the work became figuring out how far that observation held up, and under what conditions it stopped working.

r001.rationale: It asks why a small network that works after pruning could not have been trained small from the start, communicating the question behind pruning after training.

r002.rationale: It describes an empirical experiment, but does not say Frankle used hypothesis testing to challenge unsubstantiated received wisdom in deep learning.

sol-6.1.text:
My approach was to take an intuition and try to turn it into a very concrete experiment. With the lottery ticket hypothesis, the question was: if you can prune a trained network down to something much smaller, why couldn’t you have trained that smaller network in the first place?

So you train a network, prune it, and then reset the surviving weights to the values they had at initialization. Can that network learn again? And the crucial comparison is whether the same architecture works when you give it a fresh random initialization. That lets you separate the importance of the structure from the importance of those particular initial weights.

That’s really how the hypothesis took shape: through a simple experiment that made a fairly vague question testable. Rather than starting with a grand explanation, you find a surprising result, check the controls, and then ask how far it holds.

r001.rationale: It asks why a network that can be pruned after training could not have been trained at the smaller size from the start, conveying the same question.

r002.rationale: It describes making a question testable through experiments and controls, but does not say this challenged received wisdom or unsubstantiated assumptions in deep learning.
